\begin{definition}[Dual Walsh character]
\lean{FABL.dualWalshCharacter}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p023-b001,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p227-b006,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p228-b008,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p228-b010
}
\label{FABL.dualWalshCharacter}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.binarySign, FABL.𝔽₂}
Let $V$ be an abelian group equipped with a vector space structure over $br/br$
replaced here by the two-element field $br?$. For each linear functional
$\psi:V\to\mathbb{F}_2$, the associated additive character is the map
$x\mapsto(-1)^{\psi(x)}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Evaluation of a dual Walsh character]
\lean{FABL.dualWalshCharacter_apply}
\label{FABL.dualWalshCharacter_apply}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.binarySign, FABL.dualWalshCharacter, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{1}
Let $V$ be an additive commutative group and a vector space over $\mathbb{F}_2$, let
$\psi$ be a linear functional on $V$, and let $x\in V$. The Walsh character associated
with $\psi$, evaluated at $x$, is the binary sign of $\psi(x)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Injectivity of the binary sign]
\lean{FABL.binarySign_injective}
\label{FABL.binarySign_injective}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.binarySign, FABL.binarySign_eq_one_iff, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{5}
The binary sign map from $\mathbb{F}_2$ to $\mathbb{R}$ is injective.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Injectivity of the dual Walsh character]
\lean{FABL.dualWalshCharacter_injective}
\label{FABL.dualWalshCharacter_injective}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.binarySign_injective, FABL.dualWalshCharacter, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{3}
Let $V$ be an additive commutative group and a vector space over $\mathbb{F}_2$. The map
sending each linear functional $\psi:V\to\mathbb{F}_2$ to its associated real-valued
Walsh character is injective.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Dual Fourier coefficient]
\lean{FABL.dualFourierCoeff}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p025-b004,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p211-b002
}
\label{FABL.dualFourierCoeff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.dualWalshCharacter, FABL.finiteAddFourierCoeff, FABL.𝔽₂}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{F}_2$, and let $f:V\to\bbr$.
For a linear functional $\psi:V\to\mathbb{F}_2$, its dual Fourier coefficient is the
finite additive Fourier coefficient of $f$ against the character
$x\mapsto(-1)^{\psi(x)}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Product of dual Walsh characters]
\lean{FABL.dualWalshCharacter_mul}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p229-b002}
\label{FABL.dualWalshCharacter_mul}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.binarySign, FABL.dualWalshCharacter, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{3}
Let $V$ be an additive commutative group and a vector space over $\mathbb{F}_2$. For any
two linear functionals $\psi,\phi:V\to\mathbb{F}_2$, the pointwise product of their
real-valued Walsh characters is the Walsh character associated with $\psi+\phi$.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{4}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $bbf_2$, and let $psi,phi$ be
linear functionals from $V$ to $bbf_2$. The uniform average over $x\in V$ of the
product of their associated sign characters is $1$ if $psi=phi$ and $0$ otherwise.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Dual Walsh basis]
\lean{FABL.dualWalshBasis}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p024-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p228-b007,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p228-b009,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p228-b010,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p228-b011
}
\label{FABL.dualWalshBasis}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.dualWalshCharacter, FABL.dualWalshCharacter_injective, FABL.𝔽₂}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{F}_2$. The characters
$x\mapsto(-1)^{\psi(x)}$, indexed by all linear functionals $\psi:V\to\mathbb{F}_2$,
form a basis of the real vector space of functions $V\to\bbr$.
\end{definition}

\difficulty{3}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{F}_2$, and let
$f,g:V\to\bbr$. Their uniform inner product satisfies the Plancherel identity
\[\mathbb{E}_{x\in V}[f(x)g(x)] = \sum_{\psi\in V^*}\widehat f(\psi)\widehat g(\psi),\]
where $V^*$ is the linear dual and each Fourier coefficient is the uniform inner product
of the function with the Walsh character associated with that functional.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Dual Fourier support]
\lean{FABL.dualFourierSupport}
\label{FABL.dualFourierSupport}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.dualFourierCoeff, FABL.𝔽₂}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over the field with two elements, and let
$f:V\to\mathbb R$. Its dual Fourier support is the set of linear functionals on $V$
whose dual Fourier coefficient for $f$ is nonzero.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Characterization of dual Fourier support]
\lean{FABL.mem_dualFourierSupport}
\label{FABL.mem_dualFourierSupport}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.dualFourierCoeff, FABL.dualFourierSupport, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{1}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{F}_2$ whose additive
structure is commutative, let $f:V\to\mathbb{R}$, and let $\psi$ be a linear functional
from $V$ to $\mathbb{F}_2$. Then $\psi$ belongs to the dual Fourier support of $f$ if
and only if the corresponding dual Fourier coefficient is nonzero.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Dual spectral sparsity]
\lean{FABL.dualSpectralSparsity}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p072-b002,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p086-b015
}
\label{FABL.dualSpectralSparsity}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.dualFourierSupport}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{F}_2$, and let $f:V\to\bbr$.
The dual spectral sparsity of $f$ is the number of linear functionals on $V$ at which
its dual Fourier coefficient is nonzero.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Dual Fourier granularity]
\lean{FABL.IsDualFourierGranular}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p072-b003,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p089-b003
}
\label{FABL.IsDualFourierGranular}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.dualFourierCoeff, FABL.𝔽₂}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{F}_2$, let $f:V\to\bbr$, and
let $\epsilon\in\bbr$. The dual Fourier coefficients of $f$ are granular at scale
$\epsilon$ if every such coefficient is an integer multiple of $\epsilon$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Changing Fourier Granularity]
\lean{FABL.IsDualFourierGranular.refine}
\label{FABL.IsDualFourierGranular.refine}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsDualFourierGranular}
\difficulty{4}
Let $V$ be a finite additive group and a vector space over $\mathbb F_2$. Suppose every
dual Fourier coefficient of a real-valued function $f$ on $V$ is an integer multiple of
$\delta$. If $q\in\mathbb Z$ and $\delta=q\varepsilon$, then every dual Fourier
coefficient of $f$ is an integer multiple of $\varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Granularity from spectral sparsity]
\lean{FABL.spectralSparsityGranularity}
\statementsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p089-b003}
\label{FABL.spectralSparsityGranularity}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.degreeFourierGranularity}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{F}_2$. For a natural number
$s$, the spectral-sparsity granularity is the degree Fourier granularity at degree
$\lfloor\log_2 s\rfloor$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Positivity of spectral sparsity granularity]
\lean{FABL.spectralSparsityGranularity_pos}
\label{FABL.spectralSparsityGranularity_pos}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.degreeFourierGranularity_pos, FABL.spectralSparsityGranularity}
\difficulty{1}
For every nonnegative integer $s$, the spectral sparsity granularity at $s$ is strictly
positive.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Real form of spectral sparsity granularity]
\lean{FABL.spectralSparsityGranularity_cast}
\label{FABL.spectralSparsityGranularity_cast}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.degreeFourierGranularity_cast, FABL.spectralSparsityGranularity}
\difficulty{1}
For every nonnegative integer $s$, the real value of the spectral sparsity granularity
is $2(2^{-1})^{\operatorname{log}_2 s}$, where $\operatorname{log}_2 s$ denotes the
integer logarithm to base $2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Scaling of Fourier granularity]
\lean{FABL.degreeFourierGranularity_cast_eq_intCast_mul_of_le}
\label{FABL.degreeFourierGranularity_cast_eq_intCast_mul_of_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.degreeFourierGranularity, FABL.degreeFourierGranularity_cast, FABL.inverse_two_pow_eq_natCast_mul_inverse_two_pow}
\difficulty{3}
For natural numbers $\ell$ and $k$ with $\ell \le k$, the Fourier granularity at level
$\ell$ equals $2^{k-\ell}$ times the Fourier granularity at level $k$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Granularity from positive dimension]
\lean{FABL.isDualFourierGranular_signValue_of_finrank_pos}
\label{FABL.isDualFourierGranular_signValue_of_finrank_pos}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsDualFourierGranular, FABL.Sign, FABL.binarySign_one, FABL.degreeFourierGranularity, FABL.degreeFourierGranularity_cast, FABL.dualFourierCoeff_eq_expect, FABL.dualWalshCharacter, FABL.dualWalshCharacter_apply, FABL.expect_sign_values_eq_int_mul_two_inv_pow, FABL.signValue, FABL.signValue_eq_neg_one_or_one, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{5}
Let $V$ be a finite vector space over $\mathbb F_2$ with positive dimension, and let
$f:V\to\{-1,1\}$. Every dual Fourier coefficient of the real-valued function associated
to $f$ is an integer multiple of $2(1/2)^{\dim V}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fourier Granularity in Dimension Zero]
\lean{FABL.isDualFourierGranular_signValue_of_finrank_zero}
\label{FABL.isDualFourierGranular_signValue_of_finrank_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsDualFourierGranular, FABL.Sign, FABL.degreeFourierGranularity, FABL.dualFourierCoeff, FABL.dualFourierCoeff_eq_expect, FABL.signValue, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{4}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over the two-element field with dimension
zero, and let $f:V\to\{\pm1\}$. Every Walsh Fourier coefficient of the real-valued
function $x\mapsto f(x)$ on the dual group of $V$ is an integer multiple of $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Restriction of a Walsh character]
\lean{FABL.dualWalshCharacter_dualRestrict}
\label{FABL.dualWalshCharacter_dualRestrict}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.dualWalshCharacter, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{1}
Let $V$ be a vector space over $br/	ext{?}$—more precisely, over the field with two
elements—and let $H$ be a subspace of $V$. For every linear functional
$\psi:V\to\mathbb{F}_2$ and every $h\in H$, the Walsh character on $H$ obtained by
restricting $\psi$ takes at $h$ the same value as the Walsh character on $V$ takes at
the image of $h$ in $V$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fourier coefficients of a subspace restriction]
\lean{FABL.dualFourierCoeff_subspaceRestriction_eq_sum_fiber}
\label{FABL.dualFourierCoeff_subspaceRestriction_eq_sum_fiber}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.dualFourierCoeff, FABL.dualFourierCoeff_eq_expect, FABL.dualWalshCharacter, FABL.dualWalshCharacter_dualRestrict, FABL.dual_fourier_expansion, FABL.expect_dualWalshCharacter_mul, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{4}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{F}_2$, let $H\le V$, let
$f:V\to\mathbb{R}$, and let $\phi$ be a linear functional on $H$. The Fourier
coefficient of the restriction of $f$ to $H$ at $\phi$ equals the sum of the Fourier
coefficients of $f$ at all linear functionals on $V$ whose restrictions to $H$ equal
$\phi$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Spectral sparsity under subspace restriction]
\lean{FABL.dualSpectralSparsity_subspaceRestriction_le}
\label{FABL.dualSpectralSparsity_subspaceRestriction_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.dualFourierCoeff_subspaceRestriction_eq_sum_fiber, FABL.dualFourierSupport, FABL.dualSpectralSparsity, FABL.mem_dualFourierSupport, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{4}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{F}_2$, let $H\le V$, and let
$f:V\to\mathbb{R}$. The number of nonzero Fourier coefficients of the restriction of $f$
to $H$ is at most the number of nonzero Fourier coefficients of $f$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Kernel of restriction to a hyperplane]
\lean{FABL.ker_dualRestrict_ker_eq_span}
\label{FABL.ker_dualRestrict_ker_eq_span}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{1}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb F_2$, and let
$\beta:V\to\mathbb F_2$ be a nonzero linear functional. The kernel of the restriction
map from linear functionals on $V$ to linear functionals on $\ker\beta$ is the
one-dimensional span of $\beta$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fibers of restriction from a hyperplane kernel]
\lean{FABL.dualRestrict_ker_fiber_iff}
\label{FABL.dualRestrict_ker_fiber_iff}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.ker_dualRestrict_ker_eq_span, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{5}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb{F}_2$, let $\beta$ be a
nonzero linear functional on $V$, and let $\psi,\gamma$ be linear functionals on $V$.
The restrictions of $\psi$ and $\gamma$ to $\ker\beta$ are equal if and only if
$\psi=\gamma$ or $\psi=\gamma+\beta$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fourier coefficient preserved on a kernel]
\lean{FABL.exists_nonzero_dualFourierCoeff_subspaceRestriction_eq}
\label{FABL.exists_nonzero_dualFourierCoeff_subspaceRestriction_eq}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.dualFourierCoeff, FABL.dualFourierCoeff_subspaceRestriction_eq_sum_fiber, FABL.dualFourierSupport, FABL.dualRestrict_ker_fiber_iff, FABL.dualSpectralSparsity, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{6}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over the field with two elements, let
$f:V\to\mathbb{R}$, and let $\gamma$ be a linear functional whose Fourier coefficient of
$f$ is nonzero. If the number of nonzero Fourier coefficients of $f$ is less than the
number of linear functionals on $V$, then there are a nonzero linear functional $\beta$
on $V$ and a linear functional $\phi$ on the kernel of $\beta$ such that the Fourier
coefficient of the restriction of $f$ to that kernel at $\phi$ equals the Fourier
coefficient of $f$ at $\gamma$.
\end{theorem}

  {pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p071-b009}
\difficulty{6}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $\mathbb F_2$, let $f:V\to\{-1,1\}$,
and let $S$ be a natural number with $2\le S$. If at most $S$ dual Fourier coefficients
of the real-valued function associated to $f$ are nonzero, then every dual Fourier
coefficient is an integer multiple of $2(1/2)^{\lfloor\log_2 S\rfloor}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Vector space and dual identification]
\lean{FABL.vectorDualEquiv}
\label{FABL.vectorDualEquiv}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.𝔽₂}
For each natural number $n$, the dot-product pairing identifies the $n$-dimensional
coordinate space over the field with two elements with its linear dual: each vector
corresponds to the linear functional given by dot product with that vector.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Evaluation of the vector dual map]
\lean{FABL.vectorDualEquiv_apply}
\label{FABL.vectorDualEquiv_apply}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.f₂DotProduct, FABL.vectorDualEquiv}
\difficulty{1}
For every natural number $n$ and vectors $\gamma,x\in\mathbb{F}_2^n$, the linear
functional associated to $\gamma$ by the standard vector-to-dual-space equivalence,
evaluated at $x$, is the dot product $\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_i x_i$ in $\mathbb{F}_2$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Vector and dual Walsh characters]
\lean{FABL.dualWalshCharacter_vectorDualEquiv}
\label{FABL.dualWalshCharacter_vectorDualEquiv}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.dualWalshCharacter, FABL.dualWalshCharacter_apply, FABL.vectorDualEquiv, FABL.vectorDualEquiv_apply, FABL.vectorWalshCharacter, FABL.vectorWalshCharacter_apply}
\difficulty{3}
For every natural number $n$ and every vector $\gamma\in\mathbb{F}_2^n$, the dual Walsh
character associated with the linear functional corresponding to $\gamma$ under the
standard dot-product identification of $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ with its dual equals the vector
Walsh character indexed by $\gamma$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fourier coefficients under the vector space duality]
\lean{FABL.dualFourierCoeff_vectorDualEquiv}
\label{FABL.dualFourierCoeff_vectorDualEquiv}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.dualFourierCoeff, FABL.dualFourierCoeff_eq_expect, FABL.dualWalshCharacter_vectorDualEquiv, FABL.vectorDualEquiv, FABL.vectorFourierCoeff, FABL.vectorFourierCoeff_eq_expect}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $f:\mathbb{F}_2^n\to\mathbb{R}$. For every
$\gamma\in\mathbb{F}_2^n$, the Fourier coefficient of $f$ at the linear functional
$x\mapsto\sum_{i=1}^n\gamma_i x_i$ equals the vector Fourier coefficient of $f$ at
$\gamma$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Equality of spectral sparsities]
\lean{FABL.dualSpectralSparsity_eq_spectralSparsity}
\label{FABL.dualSpectralSparsity_eq_spectralSparsity}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.dualFourierCoeff_vectorDualEquiv, FABL.dualSpectralSparsity, FABL.mem_dualFourierSupport, FABL.mem_vectorFourierSupport, FABL.spectralSparsity, FABL.spectralSparsity_eq_card_vectorFourierSupport, FABL.vectorDualEquiv}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number and let $f:\mathbb{F}_2^n\to\mathbb{R}$. The number of
nonzero vector Fourier coefficients of $f$ equals the number of nonzero Fourier
coefficients indexed by linear functionals on $\mathbb{F}_2^n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fourier coefficient preserved on a subspace kernel]
\lean{FABL.exists_nonzero_vectorFourierCoeff_subspaceRestriction_eq}
\label{FABL.exists_nonzero_vectorFourierCoeff_subspaceRestriction_eq}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.dualFourierCoeff, FABL.dualFourierCoeff_vectorDualEquiv, FABL.dualFourierSupport, FABL.dualSpectralSparsity, FABL.dualSpectralSparsity_eq_spectralSparsity, FABL.exists_nonzero_dualFourierCoeff_subspaceRestriction_eq, FABL.mem_dualFourierSupport, FABL.mem_vectorFourierSupport, FABL.spectralSparsity, FABL.vectorDualEquiv, FABL.vectorFourierCoeff, FABL.vectorFourierSupport, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f$ be a real-valued function on the $n$-dimensional
vector space over the field with two elements, and let $\gamma$ be a frequency with
nonzero Fourier coefficient. If the number of nonzero Fourier coefficients of $f$ is
less than $2^n$, then there exist a nonzero linear functional $\beta$ and a linear
functional $\phi$ on its kernel such that the Fourier coefficient of the restriction of
$f$ to that kernel at $\phi$ equals the Fourier coefficient of $f$ at $\gamma$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Fourier coefficient preserved on a hyperplane]
\lean{FABL.exists_nonzero_vectorFourierCoeff_hyperplaneRestriction_eq}
\label{FABL.exists_nonzero_vectorFourierCoeff_hyperplaneRestriction_eq}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.dualFourierCoeff, FABL.exists_nonzero_vectorFourierCoeff_subspaceRestriction_eq, FABL.spectralSparsity, FABL.vectorDualEquiv, FABL.vectorFourierCoeff, FABL.vectorFourierSupport, FABL.𝔽₂}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f$ be a real-valued function on the $n$-dimensional
vector space over the field with two elements, and let $\gamma$ be a frequency with
nonzero Fourier coefficient. If the number of nonzero Fourier coefficients of $f$ is
less than $2^n$, then there exist a nonzero vector $\beta$ and a linear functional
$\phi$ on the hyperplane defined by the linear equation $\beta\cdot x=0$ such that the
Fourier coefficient of the restriction of $f$ to this hyperplane at $\phi$ equals the
Fourier coefficient of $f$ at $\gamma$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Equivalence of two Fourier granularity conditions]
\lean{FABL.isDualFourierGranular_iff_isVectorFourierGranular}
\label{FABL.isDualFourierGranular_iff_isVectorFourierGranular}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsDualFourierGranular, FABL.IsVectorFourierGranular, FABL.dualFourierCoeff_vectorDualEquiv, FABL.isVectorFourierGranular_iff, FABL.vectorDualEquiv}
\difficulty{4}
For every natural number $n$, real-valued function $f$ on the vector space $\mathbb
F_2^n$, and real number $\varepsilon$, the following are equivalent: every dual Fourier
coefficient of $f$ is an integer multiple of $\varepsilon$, and every Fourier
coefficient of the corresponding function on the sign cube is an integer multiple of
$\varepsilon$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Granularity from bounded spectral sparsity]
\lean{FABL.isVectorFourierGranular_signValue_of_spectralSparsity_le}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p089-b003}
\label{FABL.isVectorFourierGranular_signValue_of_spectralSparsity_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsVectorFourierGranular, FABL.Sign, FABL.dualSpectralSparsity_eq_spectralSparsity, FABL.isDualFourierGranular_iff_isVectorFourierGranular, FABL.isDualFourierGranular_signValue_of_dualSpectralSparsity_le, FABL.signValue, FABL.spectralSparsity, FABL.spectralSparsityGranularity}
\difficulty{3}
Let $S\ge 2$ be an integer and let $f$ map the $n$-dimensional cube over $bf_2$ to
signs. If the number of nonzero vector Fourier coefficients of the real-valued function
$x\mapsto f(x)$ is at most $S$, then this function is vector Fourier granular with
granularity $2^{1-\lfloor\log_2 S\rfloor}$; that is, each Fourier coefficient on the
sign cube is an integer multiple of this number.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{1}
Let $f$ map the $n$-dimensional cube over $bf_2$ to signs, and suppose the spectral
sparsity $s$ of the real-valued function $x\mapsto f(x)$ is greater than $1$. Then this
function is vector Fourier granular with granularity $2^{1-\lfloor\log_2 s\rfloor}$;
each Fourier coefficient on the sign cube is an integer multiple of this number.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Parseval identity for sign-valued functions]
\lean{FABL.sum_sq_vectorFourierCoeff_signValue_eq_one}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p025-b006}
\label{FABL.sum_sq_vectorFourierCoeff_signValue_eq_one}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.signValue, FABL.signValue_eq_neg_one_or_one, FABL.vectorFourierCoeff, FABL.vector_plancherel}
\difficulty{4}
Let $n$ be a natural number, and let $f$ map the $n$-dimensional vector space over
$\\mathbb F_2$ to signs. Then the sum, over all vectors $\\gamma$ in that space, of the
squares of the binary Fourier coefficients of the real-valued function $x\\mapsto f(x)$
is $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Sparsity and granularity inequality]
\lean{FABL.spectralSparsity_mul_granularity_sq_le_one}
\label{FABL.spectralSparsity_mul_granularity_sq_le_one}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.isVectorFourierGranular_iff, FABL.isVectorFourierGranular_signValue_spectralSparsity, FABL.mem_vectorFourierSupport, FABL.signValue, FABL.spectralSparsity, FABL.spectralSparsityGranularity, FABL.spectralSparsityGranularity_pos, FABL.spectralSparsity_eq_card_vectorFourierSupport, FABL.sum_sq_vectorFourierCoeff_signValue_eq_one, FABL.vectorFourierCoeff, FABL.vectorFourierSupport}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $f$ be a function from the $n$-dimensional
vector space over $\mathbb F_2$ to the signs. If the spectral sparsity $s$ of the
real-valued function obtained from $f$ is greater than $1$, then $s$ times the square of
the spectral sparsity granularity at $s$ is at most $1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Spectral sparsity avoids its parameter]
\lean{FABL.spectralSparsity_ne_of_granularity_bound}
\label{FABL.spectralSparsity_ne_of_granularity_bound}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.signValue, FABL.spectralSparsity, FABL.spectralSparsityGranularity, FABL.spectralSparsity_mul_granularity_sq_le_one}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n,s\in\mathbb N$, and let $f:\mathbb F_2^n\to\{\pm1\}$. Suppose $1<s$ and
$1<s\bigl(2(1/2)^{\lfloor\log_2 s\rfloor}\bigr)^2$, where $\lfloor\log_2 s\rfloor$
denotes the integer logarithm used to define the granularity. Then the number of nonzero
vector Fourier coefficients of $x\mapsto f(x)$ is not $s$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Spectral sparsity avoids nine]
\lean{FABL.spectralSparsity_ne_nine}
\label{FABL.spectralSparsity_ne_nine}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.IsVectorFourierGranular, FABL.Sign, FABL.degreeFourierGranularity, FABL.isVectorFourierGranular_iff, FABL.isVectorFourierGranular_signValue_spectralSparsity, FABL.mem_vectorFourierSupport, FABL.signValue, FABL.spectralSparsity, FABL.spectralSparsityGranularity, FABL.spectralSparsity_eq_card_vectorFourierSupport, FABL.sum_sq_vectorFourierCoeff_signValue_eq_one, FABL.vectorFourierCoeff, FABL.vectorFourierSupport}
\difficulty{6}
For every dimension $n$ and every function $f:\mathbb F_2^n\to\{\pm1\}$, the number of
nonzero vector Fourier coefficients of the real-valued function $x\mapsto f(x)$ is not
equal to $9$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Exceptional spectral sparsities]
\lean{FABL.spectralSparsity_not_mem_exceptional}
\label{FABL.spectralSparsity_not_mem_exceptional}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.Sign, FABL.degreeFourierGranularity, FABL.signValue, FABL.spectralSparsity, FABL.spectralSparsityGranularity, FABL.spectralSparsity_ne_nine, FABL.spectralSparsity_ne_of_granularity_bound}
\difficulty{4}
For every dimension $n$ and every function $f:\mathbb F_2^n\to\{\pm1\}$, the number of
nonzero vector Fourier coefficients of the real-valued function $x\mapsto f(x)$ does not
belong to $\{2,3,5,6,7,9\}$.
\end{theorem}
